title: Saint Augustine's Philosophy and Theology
orientation: Russell examines Saint Augustine of Hippo (354-430) under three headings: his pure philosophy of time in the Confessions, his philosophy of history in The City of God, and his theory of salvation against the Pelagians. The chapter matters because Augustine is, for Russell, the first Christian thinker whose speculative philosophy is genuinely original rather than a mere overlay of Platonism on Scripture, and because the doctrines worked out here -- creation, time, the two cities, predestination -- shaped Western Christendom's self-understanding for a millennium.
historical_background: Augustine, bishop of Hippo in Roman North Africa, spent his episcopate contending with the Donatist, Manichaean, and Pelagian controversies. The City of God was occasioned by the sack of Rome by Alaric's Goths in 410, which pagans blamed on the abandonment of the old gods; Augustine wrote it, gradually between 412 and 427, as a reply that grew into a full Christian philosophy of history. The Pelagian controversy occupied much of his later career and was formally settled against Pelagius's followers only at the Council of Orange in 529, a century after Augustine's death.
philosophical_problems: What is time, and how can it be reconciled with an eternal, timeless God who creates the world?
Was the world created out of pre-existing matter (the Greek view) or out of nothing (the Scriptural view), and what follows from each?
How can a providential 'sacred history' make sense of catastrophe (the sack of Rome) without abandoning belief in a just and omnipotent God?
If Adam's sin corrupted all his descendants, how can God justly damn unbaptized infants, and how can salvation by grace be reconciled with human free will and moral responsibility?
What is the proper relation between the earthly city (the State) and the City of God (the Church)?

philosophers_discussed.name: Saint Augustine
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's sole primary subject: Russell treats his theory of time as a genuine philosophical achievement, his City of God as historically transformative if intellectually derivative, and his anti-Pelagian doctrine of predestination as his most influential but most 'ferocious' teaching.

philosophers_discussed.name: Plato
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as holding, with Aristotle, that God is an 'artificer' who imposes form on eternal, pre-existing matter rather than a true Creator; also praised at length by Augustine in Book VIII of The City of God as the greatest of the philosophers, nearest to Christianity on God and immortality.

philosophers_discussed.name: Aristotle
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Grouped with Plato as holding the Greek view that substance is eternal and uncreated, with only form due to God's will; in The City of God, ranked by Augustine as Plato's inferior but far above other philosophers.

philosophers_discussed.name: Origen
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Contrasted with Augustine as an earlier Christian philosopher in whom Christianity and Platonism 'lie side by side' without interpenetrating; also criticized by Augustine for holding that souls were given bodies as a punishment, and for denying that hell is eternal.

philosophers_discussed.name: Plotinus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named by Augustine, following a common view, as the interpreter who 'understood Plato the best of any'; Russell notes the Neoplatonist background to Augustine's discussion of angels and demons.

philosophers_discussed.name: Pelagius
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A Welsh (British) ecclesiastic who taught free will, denied original sin, and held that virtuous action earns heaven by its own moral effort; his doctrine, opposed by Augustine, was declared heretical, though it retained temporary support among Eastern theologians.

philosophers_discussed.name: Immanuel Kant
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Invoked by Russell as a later parallel: Augustine's subjective theory of time is judged 'a better and clearer statement than Kant's' of a subjectivist view of time that became widely accepted after Kant.

philosophers_discussed.name: Rene Descartes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Invoked by Russell to show that Augustine, in the Soliloquia, anticipated both the cogito ('I know that I think') and Descartes's reply to Gassendi's ambulo ergo sum.

core_concepts.name: Creation ex nihilo
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The doctrine that God made the universe out of absolutely nothing, rather than shaping some pre-existing raw material, as older Greek thought had assumed.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine, taught in the Old Testament and defended by Augustine against Manichaean and Greek views, that God created substance itself, not merely order and arrangement imposed on eternal, pre-existing matter.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It marks a decisive break from Greek metaphysics, where God is an artificer working on eternal matter, and it forces the question of what, if anything, existed 'before' creation -- the problem that leads directly into Augustine's theory of time.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Rooted in Genesis; defended by Augustine as a requirement of Christian orthodoxy against both the Manichaeans and residual Greek assumptions.
examples: Augustine's rejection of the Manichaean objector who asks why God did not create the world sooner
objections: The Greek philosophical view that creation out of nothing is impossible, which recurred in Christian times and, Russell notes, led toward pantheism
competing_positions: Plato and Aristotle's view of God as artificer shaping eternal matter
Pantheism (later fully developed by Spinoza), which denies any real distinction between God and the world
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Became settled Christian orthodoxy; the alternative view recurred among mystics, who, Russell notes, have historically found it hard to stay orthodox because they resist placing the world wholly outside God.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly theological; underwrites Augustine's argument that Genesis, not Greek metaphysics, must govern Christian cosmology.

core_concepts.name: Augustine's relativistic (subjective) theory of time
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Augustine argues that only the present moment truly exists; the past exists only as present memory, and the future only as present expectation. Time, on this view, is something the mind does, not an independent framework the world sits inside.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that there are properly speaking three 'presents' -- a present of things past (memory), a present of things present (sight), and a present of things future (expectation) -- and that time is therefore subjective, existing in the created, remembering, expecting mind rather than as an objective container that could have existed 'before' Creation.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It lets Augustine answer the Manichaean taunt 'why did God not create the world sooner?' by dissolving the question: since time itself began with creation, there was no 'sooner' for the world to have been created in.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in Book XI of the Confessions, in response to a hypothetical objector demanding why the Creation did not occur earlier.
examples: 'What, then, is time? If no one asks of me, I know; if I wish to explain to him who asks, I know not.'
The identification of the 'three times' with memory, sight, and expectation
objections: Russell himself disagrees with the theory insofar as it makes time purely mental
competing_positions: The Greek/Platonic-Aristotelian assumption of an objective, presupposed time within which creation occurs
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell judges it a clearer anticipation of Kant's subjectivist theory of time than anything in Greek philosophy, and situates it within a broader current of subjectivism running from Protagoras and Socrates through to Descartes's cogito, which Augustine's Soliloquia also anticipates.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Underwrites the theological claim that God is timelessly eternal and that time itself is a created, not an eternal, feature of reality.

core_concepts.name: Pantheism
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The view that God and the world are not really separate -- that everything that exists is, in some sense, part of God.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that God and the world are not distinct, so that everything in the world is part of God; developed most fully, in Russell's later account, by Spinoza, but attractive to mystics generally.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell uses it as the foil against which Augustine's insistence on creation ex nihilo, and his freedom from mystical difficulty about the world's separateness from God, stands out.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Recurs, per Russell, as a natural consequence of the Greek view that creation from nothing is impossible.
competing_positions: Augustine's orthodox insistence, following Genesis, that the world is created and stands outside God
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: A recurring temptation for Christian mystics, who have historically found orthodoxy on this point difficult to maintain.

core_concepts.name: The City of God and the earthly city (the two cities)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Augustine imagines all of history as the story of two intermingled 'cities' or communities: one belonging to God and destined for eternal reward, the other belonging to the world (and ultimately to the Devil) and destined for eternal punishment. In this life the two are mixed together and cannot be told apart with certainty; only at the end will they be separated.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A providential scheme of history in which the elect (predestined for salvation, symbolized by Abel) belong to the pilgrim 'City of God,' and the reprobate (symbolized by Cain) belong to the earthly city doomed to eternal torment with Satan; in this life the two cities are commingled, but they will be definitively separated at the Last Judgement.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It supplied the theoretical justification, throughout the Middle Ages, for the claim that the State should be subordinate to the Church in religious matters, since only the Church truly represents the City of God on earth.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed across The City of God (412-427) in answer to pagans who blamed the sack of Rome (410) on the abandonment of the old gods.
examples: Cain belonging to the city of the Devil, Abel to the City of God
Augustine's argument that Christians who suffered in the sack of Rome have no right to complain, since worldly loss cannot touch what truly matters
competing_positions: The pagan view that Rome prospered under Jupiter's protection and fell once the old gods were abandoned
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell traces its influence through the medieval struggles of Church and Empire, and draws his own analogy to Marx's philosophy of history (Yahweh/Dialectical Materialism, the Messiah/Marx, the elect/the Proletariat, the Church/the Communist Party, the Second Coming/the Revolution), presented explicitly as Russell's own device for explaining Marxism's emotional appeal, not as a claim Augustine himself made.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political and religious: became, in Russell's account, the doctrinal basis for the medieval claim that secular rulers must be submissive to the Church, a position realized far more fully in the weak Western Empire than in the strong Byzantine East.

core_concepts.name: Original sin and predestination (the anti-Pelagian doctrine of salvation)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Because Adam and Eve sinned, all their descendants inherit a corrupted nature and deserve eternal damnation; no one can, by their own effort, be virtuous enough to earn salvation. God, however, freely and unaccountably chooses some people (the elect) to receive the grace that saves them, while leaving the rest to the damnation everyone equally deserves.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that Adam's sin corrupted all humanity, that all deserve eternal damnation (including unbaptized infants), that no one can abstain from sin without God's grace, and that God, by an unmotivated choice not based on merit, elects certain baptized persons to salvation while leaving the rest justly damned -- damnation displaying God's justice, salvation His mercy.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It was Augustine's answer to Pelagius's claim that virtuous moral effort alone could earn salvation, and it became, via Calvin, the doctrine of predestination central to Reformed Protestantism, while being explicitly rejected in this extreme form by the later Catholic Church.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Worked out across Augustine's controversial writings against Pelagius and his followers (the Pelagian controversy), and grounded, in Augustine's own reading, in the Pauline Epistle to the Romans.
examples: Augustine's claim, in the Confessions, to have been guilty of sins even in the cradle
The doctrine that unbaptized infants who die are damned to hell
objections: Russell notes the one difficulty that genuinely troubled Augustine himself: if original sin passes from Adam, the soul as well as the body must be propagated by the parents, though sin belongs to the soul, not the body -- a problem Augustine leaves undecided since Scripture is silent
competing_positions: Pelagius's doctrine of free will and salvation by moral effort
Semi-Pelagianism, a weakened compromise position condemned at the Council of Orange (529)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Revived by Calvin at the Reformation; its eschatology, if not its full theocratic doctrine, remained influential among Anabaptists, Fifth Monarchy Men, and Quakers.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly theological, with Russell noting its influence on the 'gloomy sense of universal guilt' he holds partly responsible for the ferocity of the medieval Church.

core_concepts.name: Pelagianism
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The rival view, held by the British monk Pelagius, that human beings have genuine free will, that there is no inherited 'original sin,' and that people earn heaven through their own virtuous moral effort.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The heresy, condemned largely through Augustine's efforts, holding that Adam's sin did not corrupt human nature, that individuals retain full free will, and that virtuous conduct is rewarded with heaven on its own merits rather than through unearned grace.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It framed the central theological battle of Augustine's later career and, though condemned, persisted in weakened ('semi-Pelagian') form for another century.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Taught by Pelagius (born Morgan), a cultivated Welsh ecclesiastic, in the early fifth century.
objections: Augustine's argument that if salvation could be earned by unaided moral effort, grace would be unnecessary and Scripture's teaching on universal sinfulness would be false
competing_positions: Augustine's doctrine of original sin, grace, and unmerited predestination
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Formally defeated at the Council of Orange in 529, though never entirely extinguished as a recurring theological temptation.

arguments.title: Why was the world not created sooner? (the timelessness of God and the creation of time)
premises: God is eternal, in the sense of being wholly timeless: for Him there is no before and after, only an eternal present.
Time itself, along with the world, was created by God; it did not pre-exist creation.
The question 'why not sooner?' presupposes an interval of time before creation in which the world could have been made earlier.
arguments.conclusion: The question is meaningless, because there was no 'sooner': time began when the world began, so there could be no earlier moment at which creation might have occurred.
arguments.explanation: Augustine imagines a Manichaean objector demanding why an all-good, all-powerful Creator delayed creation. His answer dissolves rather than answers the question: since 'before' and 'after' only make sense within time, and time itself is a created feature of the world, asking why God waited assumes exactly the framework (pre-existing time) that His timeless eternity rules out.
implications: Establishes that God stands wholly outside the created order of time, not merely at its earliest point.
Sets up Augustine's further claim that time is best understood subjectively, through memory and expectation, since it cannot be an independent framework existing 'before' any created mind.

arguments.title: The subjectivity of time (the three presents)
premises: Only the present moment can be said truly to exist; the present itself is a mere instant that vanishes as it is measured.
Yet we undeniably speak meaningfully of past and future.
Past and future can only be grasped as present facts: the past as present memory, the future as present expectation.
arguments.conclusion: There are, properly speaking, three 'presents' -- a present of things past (memory), a present of things present (sight), and a present of things future (expectation) -- and time itself exists in the created mind, which remembers, attends, and expects, rather than as an independent framework.
arguments.explanation: Augustine confesses he cannot resolve every difficulty this raises, but the gist of his solution is that time is fundamentally mental: without a created being that remembers and anticipates, there could be no time, and so it is meaningless to speak of time 'before' Creation.
objections: Russell states his own disagreement in so far as the theory makes time something purely mental, though he still regards it as a very able theory and 'a great advance on anything to be found on the subject in Greek philosophy.'
implications: Anticipates Kant's subjectivist theory of time, which Russell judges Augustine states more clearly.
Belongs to a broader current of philosophical subjectivism Russell traces from Protagoras and Socrates through to Augustine's own anticipation, in the Soliloquia, of Descartes's cogito.

arguments.title: The justice of arbitrary election (the anti-Pelagian doctrine of predestination)
premises: All humanity inherited Adam's corruption and guilt, and so all deserve eternal damnation, including unbaptized infants.
No one can, by their own unaided moral effort, abstain from sin or earn salvation.
God, by grace alone, elects certain baptized persons to salvation, for no reason grounded in their own merit or demerit.
arguments.conclusion: Damnation of the reprobate displays God's justice (since all deserve it), while salvation of the elect displays His mercy (since none of them earned it); both equally display His goodness, and the reprobate have no ground of complaint since they are only receiving what all deserve.
arguments.explanation: Russell notes that Augustine reaches this position by treating Saint Paul's Epistle to the Romans 'as a lawyer treats the law,' extracting from isolated texts the fullest possible meaning; one comes away persuaded not that Paul necessarily believed exactly what Augustine deduces, but that certain texts, taken in isolation, can be made to yield it.
objections: It may seem shocking that infants who die unbaptized should be damned by a good God, though Russell notes this did not trouble Augustine's contemporaries as much as it strikes modern readers.

Augustine himself was troubled by one difficulty he could not resolve: since sin belongs to the soul rather than the body, original sin's inheritance implies the soul, and not only the body, is propagated by the parents -- a point he leaves undecided because Scripture is silent on it.
implications: Became the doctrinal basis later revived by Calvin as predestination, and rejected in this extreme form by the later Catholic Church.
Russell attributes much of the 'ferocity' of the medieval Church's sense of universal guilt to this doctrine.

key_distinctions: Creation ex nihilo (Scriptural) vs. God as artificer shaping eternal, pre-existing matter (Greek/Platonic-Aristotelian)
Objective time as an independent framework vs. Augustine's subjective time as a feature of the remembering, expecting mind
The earthly city vs. the City of God, commingled in this life but separated at the Last Judgement
Salvation earned by moral effort (Pelagius) vs. salvation as unearned, unmotivated grace (Augustine)
Theocratic Erastianism (Church subject to State) vs. Augustine's doctrine that the State must be submissive to the Church in religious matters
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell contrasts Augustine with Origen, in whom Christianity and Platonism merely 'lie side by side'; Augustine, by contrast, is driven to original thinking precisely because Platonism, in places, conflicts with Genesis. The City of God contains an extended, admiring treatment of Plato (ranked above all other philosophers, including the materialists Thales, Anaximenes, the Stoics, and Epicurus) and a more qualified treatment of Aristotle, alongside criticism of Neoplatonist views on angels, demons, and (via Origen) the reason souls are embodied.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell credits Augustine's theory of time with anticipating Kant's subjectivist theory of time more clearly than anything in Greek philosophy, and his cogito-like remarks in the Soliloquia with anticipating Descartes, including Descartes's reply to Gassendi's ambulo ergo sum. The doctrine of predestination was revived by Calvin at the Reformation. Russell also draws his own explicit analogy between Augustine's Christian scheme of sacred history and Marx's philosophy of history, presented as Russell's device for explaining the emotional force of Marxist eschatology to readers with a Christian or Jewish upbringing, not as an Augustinian claim.
political_social_context: The City of God was written to answer the pagan charge that Rome's sack by the Goths in 410 resulted from abandoning the old gods, and it developed into the doctrinal foundation for the medieval claim that secular rulers must submit to the Church in religious matters. Russell notes this ideal was realized far more fully in the weak Western medieval monarchies than in the strong Byzantine East, where the Church remained subordinate to the emperor.
religion_science_culture_context: The chapter surveys the Donatist, Manichaean, and Pelagian controversies that occupied Augustine's career, his defense of the Septuagint's divine inspiration alongside the Hebrew text against Saint Jerome's Vulgate translation, and his attack on the 'new Academicians' (sceptics) for doubting the certain knowledge available through the Church.
russell_presentation: Russell divides his treatment into pure philosophy, philosophy of history, and soteriology, and his evaluations differ sharply across the three. He rates Augustine highly as a philosopher of time, calling the theory 'a great advance on anything to be found on the subject in Greek philosophy' and clearer than Kant's later subjectivist account, while explicitly registering his own disagreement with making time purely mental. He treats The City of God as a work that 'composes itself... into something better than at first appears on rereading,' historically transformative for the medieval Church-State relationship, but intellectually containing 'little that is fundamentally original,' since its eschatology is Jewish, its predestination doctrine Pauline, and its distinction of sacred and profane history already present in the Old Testament -- Augustine's achievement, in Russell's reading, was synthesis and application to his own age's crisis, not invention. Russell is most severe on the Pelagian controversy, calling the resulting doctrine 'this ferocious doctrine' and attributing much of what is 'most ferocious in the medieval Church' to Augustine's own 'gloomy sense of universal guilt'; he closes the chapter by remarking, pointedly, that it is strange the last intellectually eminent men before the Dark Ages were absorbed not in saving civilization but in 'preaching the merit of virginity and the damnation of unbaptized infants.'
critical_context: Russell's own analogy between Augustine's providential scheme of history and Marx's philosophy of history (and, more briefly, Nazi ideology) is explicitly Russell's own interpretive device for a twentieth-century audience -- a 'dictionary' he constructs to explain the psychological force of Marxist eschatology -- and should not be read as a claim Augustine himself made or anticipated.
key_takeaways: Augustine argues time itself began with Creation, so the question 'why did God not create the world sooner?' is meaningless, since there was no 'sooner' in which to act.

His theory of time as subjective -- existing in memory (the present of things past) and expectation (the present of things future) -- is judged by Russell a clearer anticipation of Kant than anything in Greek philosophy, though Russell rejects making time purely mental.

The City of God answers the pagan charge that abandoning the old gods caused Rome's fall, and develops a scheme of two commingled cities (earthly and heavenly) that became the doctrinal basis for medieval claims of Church supremacy over the State.

Against Pelagius's doctrine of free will and salvation by merit, Augustine taught that all humanity inherits Adam's guilt, that grace alone (not merit) saves the elect, and that damnation is justly deserved by all -- a position Russell calls 'ferocious' and later revived by Calvin.

Russell judges Augustine's philosophy of history to contain little that is fundamentally original (its elements are Jewish, Pauline, and Old Testament in origin), crediting him instead with synthesizing them to fit the crisis of his own age.
Russell explicitly frames his comparison of Augustinian and Marxist eschatology as his own interpretive analogy, not a claim about Augustine's own intentions.
study_notes:
The clearest way to organize this chapter is around Russell's own three-part division: pure philosophy (time), philosophy of history (The City of God), and soteriology (the Pelagian controversy). Each section shows a different side of Augustine, and Russell's evaluation shifts accordingly -- admiring in the first, mixed in the second, and highly critical in the third. It is worth tracking why: the theory of time is, for Russell, an original piece of reasoning that stands on its own philosophical merits regardless of its theological motivation; The City of God is judged by its historical influence and its synthetic power rather than its originality; and the anti-Pelagian doctrine is judged by its moral and human consequences, which Russell finds genuinely harmful.

A second thread worth isolating is how tightly Augustine's pure philosophy is yoked to Scriptural constraint. Russell stresses that Augustine is 'the first of a long line whose purely speculative views are influenced by the necessity of agreeing with Scripture' -- unlike Origen, in whom Platonism and Christianity sit side by side without interacting. This matters because it explains why Augustine's philosophy of time is not simply borrowed Platonism: the doctrine of creation ex nihilo, forced on him by Genesis, is precisely what makes the old Greek question 'why not sooner?' pressing, and precisely what forces him toward an original, non-Greek answer.

Finally, notice how the chapter's three sections connect to each other causally as well as thematically. The doctrine of creation ex nihilo (section I) underwrites the idea that history itself is not eternal but has a beginning and a providential shape (section II); and the belief that Adam's fall introduced sin and death into that history (also from section II) is exactly what generates the theological problem -- inherited guilt and unmerited grace -- that Augustine works out against Pelagius (section III). The chapter is not three separate essays but one argument moving from metaphysics, through history, to soteriology.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that God made the universe from nothing at all, rather than shaping already-existing material.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The Scriptural doctrine, defended by Augustine against Greek philosophy and Manichaeism, that God created substance itself and not merely order imposed on eternal matter.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Augustine's name for the community of the elect, the true, invisible society of the saved, as opposed to the ordinary earthly societies of this world.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In Augustine's philosophy of history, the pilgrim society of the predestined elect, commingled in this life with the earthly city but destined to be eternally separated from it at the Last Judgement.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that God has already decided, in advance and without regard to anyone's merit, who will be saved and who will be damned.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Augustine's doctrine that God elects certain persons to salvation by grace alone, an unmotivated choice not grounded in the merits or demerits of the elect, developed chiefly against Pelagius.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The rival Christian teaching that people have full free will and can earn their way to heaven through their own good conduct, without needing unearned divine grace.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The heresy taught by Pelagius, denying inherited original sin and affirming that virtuous action, freely chosen, is rewarded with salvation on its own merits; condemned largely through Augustine's efforts and finally at the Council of Orange (529).

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A dualistic religion, which Augustine himself once followed, teaching that the world is a battleground between a good and an evil principle.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A dualist religious movement against which Augustine directed much controversial writing; in this chapter, the source of the objector's challenge -- why did God not create the world sooner? -- that prompts Augustine's theory of time.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The belief that God and the universe are really the same thing, so that everything that exists is part of God.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The view, developed most fully by Spinoza and attractive to many mystics, that denies a real distinction between God and the created world; contrasted by Russell with Augustine's orthodox insistence on creation ex nihilo.

questions.prompt: What three topics does Russell say he will discuss in Saint Augustine's work in this chapter?
questions.answer: His pure philosophy, particularly the theory of time; his philosophy of history as developed in The City of God; and his theory of salvation as propounded against the Pelagians.
questions.explanation: Russell states this three-part structure explicitly at the start of the chapter and organizes his discussion accordingly.

questions.prompt: How does Augustine answer the objection 'why did God not create the world sooner'?
questions.answer: By arguing that there was no 'sooner': time itself began with the creation of the world, so it is meaningless to imagine an earlier moment when creation could have occurred, since God is timelessly eternal and stands outside the stream of time altogether.
questions.explanation: This is the central move of Augustine's theory of time in Book XI of the Confessions, and it leads directly into his subjectivist account of time as memory and expectation.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, which two ancient philosophers held that God is an 'artificer' shaping eternal, pre-existing matter, rather than a true Creator?
questions.explanation: Russell contrasts their view of creation with the Scriptural doctrine of creation ex nihilo that Augustine defends against them.

questions.prompt: Contrast Augustine's doctrine of salvation with Pelagius's.
questions.answer: Pelagius held that human beings retain free will, that original sin is not truly inherited, and that virtuous moral effort earns heaven on its own merits. Augustine held that Adam's sin corrupted all humanity, that no one can avoid sin without God's grace, and that salvation is granted by God's unmotivated choice (predestination) rather than by merit.
questions.explanation: This contrast is the substance of the Pelagian controversy, which Russell treats as Augustine's most influential, if also most 'ferocious,' theological legacy.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Augustine's argument that damnation of the reprobate and salvation of the elect both display God's goodness.
questions.answer: All humanity inherited Adam's guilt and so all equally deserve eternal damnation; no one can, by unaided effort, avoid sin; God freely and without regard to merit chooses some (the elect) to receive saving grace, while leaving the rest to the damnation all deserve; therefore damnation displays God's justice (since it is deserved) while salvation displays His mercy (since it is unearned), and both equally display His goodness.
questions.explanation: Russell presents this as the core structure of Augustine's anti-Pelagian doctrine, developed from a close, lawyerlike reading of Saint Paul's Epistle to the Romans.

questions.prompt: What event prompted Augustine to write The City of God, and what pagan argument was it written to answer?
questions.answer: The sack of Rome by the Goths in 410. Pagans argued that Rome had prospered under the protection of Jupiter and the old gods, and that its fall was punishment for abandoning them; Augustine's book was his answer, which grew into a full Christian philosophy of history.
questions.explanation: Russell frames The City of God as fundamentally an apologetic response to this specific historical crisis before it develops into a broader theory of sacred and profane history.

questions.prompt: What one intellectual difficulty does Russell say genuinely troubled Augustine about the doctrine of original sin?
questions.answer: Since original sin is inherited from Adam, and sin belongs to the soul rather than the body, it seems to follow that the soul, as well as the body, must be propagated by the parents -- a conclusion Augustine found difficult, and which he ultimately left undecided since Scripture is silent on the matter.
questions.explanation: Russell notes this is not the difficulty a modern reader might expect (the damnation of unbaptized infants did not trouble Augustine as much), which highlights how differently Augustine's moral priorities were structured from a modern reader's.

flashcards.front: What are the three topics Russell organizes this chapter around?
flashcards.back: Augustine's theory of time (pure philosophy), his philosophy of history in The City of God, and his theory of salvation against the Pelagians.

flashcards.front: What does 'creation ex nihilo' mean, and why did Augustine defend it?
flashcards.back: Creation out of nothing rather than from pre-existing matter; Augustine defended it as required by Genesis, against the Greek view of God as an artificer shaping eternal matter.

flashcards.front: According to Augustine, why is the question 'why did God not create the world sooner?' meaningless?
flashcards.back: Because time itself began with Creation; there was no 'sooner,' since God is timelessly eternal and stands outside time altogether.
A present of things past (memory), a present of things present (sight), and a present of things future (expectation).

flashcards.front: Which later philosopher's theory of time does Russell say Augustine's anticipates and, in his view, states more clearly?
Which later philosopher's cogito did Augustine anticipate in the Soliloquia?
flashcards.back: Rene Descartes's cogito ('I know that I think'), including his reply to Gassendi's ambulo ergo sum.

flashcards.front: What event prompted Augustine to write The City of God?
flashcards.back: The sack of Rome by the Goths in 410, which pagans blamed on the abandonment of the old gods.

flashcards.front: What are the 'two cities' in The City of God?
flashcards.back: The earthly city and the City of God -- commingled in this life, to be separated at the Last Judgement into the reprobate and the predestined elect.

flashcards.front: Whom does Augustine rank as the greatest of the philosophers in The City of God, and why?
flashcards.back: Plato, because he held that God is not any bodily thing, that all things derive their being from something immutable, and that perception is not the source of truth -- unlike the materialist philosophers.

flashcards.front: Who was Pelagius, and what did he teach?
flashcards.back: A cultivated Welsh ecclesiastic (born Morgan) who taught free will, denied inherited original sin, and held that virtuous moral effort earns heaven on its own merit.

flashcards.front: What is Augustine's doctrine of predestination?
flashcards.back: That God elects certain persons to salvation by grace alone, an unmotivated choice unrelated to merit; damnation of the rest displays God's justice, salvation of the elect His mercy.

flashcards.front: Which later Reformer revived Augustine's doctrine of predestination?
At which council was semi-Pelagianism finally condemned, and when?
What does Russell say is the one intellectual difficulty that genuinely troubled Augustine about original sin?
flashcards.back: Whether the soul, like the body, must be propagated by the parents, since sin belongs to the soul rather than the body -- a question he left undecided.

flashcards.front: How does Russell judge the originality of The City of God's philosophy of history?
flashcards.back: He judges it to contain little that is fundamentally original -- its eschatology is Jewish, its predestination doctrine Pauline -- crediting Augustine instead with synthesizing these elements to fit the crisis of his own age.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, what does Augustine's theory of time hold about the past and the future?
options: They exist independently of any mind
They can only be understood as present facts: memory and expectation
They do not exist in any sense
They exist only for God, not for human beings
quiz.explanation: Augustine's solution to the puzzle of time is that past and future can only be thought of as present: 'past' is memory and 'future' is expectation, both present facts.

quiz.prompt: What event directly prompted Saint Augustine to write The City of God?
options: The sack of Rome by the Goths in 410
quiz.explanation: Pagans blamed the sack of Rome on the abandonment of the old gods; The City of God was Augustine's reply.
quiz.related_concept: The City of God and the earthly city

quiz.prompt: Russell judges Augustine's theory of time to be a great advance on anything found in Greek philosophy on the subject.
quiz.explanation: Russell states explicitly that the theory 'is a great advance on anything to be found on the subject in Greek philosophy,' though he personally disagrees with making time purely mental.

quiz.prompt: Which philosopher does Russell say Augustine's theory of time anticipates and states more clearly than that philosopher himself?
quiz.explanation: Russell writes that Augustine's theory 'contains a better and clearer statement than Kant's of the subjective theory of time.'

quiz.prompt: What did Pelagius teach that Augustine opposed?
options: That the world was created out of nothing
That free will and moral effort alone, without inherited original sin, could earn salvation
That the Church should be subject to the State
quiz.explanation: Pelagius believed in free will, questioned original sin, and held that virtuous action earned heaven as a reward for one's own moral effort.

quiz.prompt: In Augustine's doctrine of predestination, what does the damnation of the reprobate display, and what does the salvation of the elect display?
options: Damnation displays cruelty; salvation displays fairness
Damnation displays God's justice; salvation displays His mercy
Neither displays anything about God's character
quiz.explanation: Russell reports Augustine's view that damnation proves God's justice (since all deserve it) while salvation proves His mercy (since it is unearned); both equally display His goodness.

quiz.prompt: Russell says Augustine's Soliloquia anticipates the philosophy of ______, including his reply to Gassendi's ambulo ergo sum.
quiz.explanation: Augustine's remarks on self-knowledge in the Soliloquia anticipate Descartes's cogito and his reply to Gassendi.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, which of the following does The City of God NOT owe primarily to Augustine's own original invention?
options: The synthesis of sacred and profane history applied to his own age's crisis
The eschatology, which is Jewish in origin
The doctrine of predestination and election, which is Pauline
The distinction between sacred and profane history, already in the Old Testament
quiz.explanation: Russell credits Augustine with the synthesis and application of these pre-existing elements to the crisis of his own time, not with inventing the elements themselves, which he traces to Jewish, Pauline, and Old Testament sources.
quiz.related_concept: The City of God and the earthly city

quiz.prompt: Match each figure to their role in this chapter: (1) Pelagius, (2) Plotinus, (3) Origen, (4) Kant -- with (A) said to have understood Plato best, (B) taught free will against original sin, (C) had a philosophy of time Russell compares to Augustine's, (D) let Christianity and Platonism lie side by side without interpenetrating.
quiz.explanation: Pelagius (B) taught free will; Plotinus (A) was said to understand Plato best; Origen (D) kept Christianity and Platonism separate; Kant (C) had a theory of time Russell compares to Augustine's.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, the doctrine of predestination worked out against Pelagius has continued to be held by the Catholic Church in its original, extreme form ever since Augustine.
quiz.explanation: Russell notes this 'ferocious doctrine... was revived by Calvin, and has since then not been held by the Catholic Church' in its extreme form.

essay_prompts.prompt: Russell praises Augustine's theory of time as a genuine philosophical achievement while sharply criticizing his doctrine of predestination as 'ferocious.' Analyze why Russell evaluates these two parts of Augustine's thought so differently, drawing on Russell's stated grounds for each judgment.
rubric: Accurately reconstructs Augustine's theory of time
Accurately reconstructs the anti-Pelagian doctrine of predestination
Identifies the distinct grounds (philosophical merit vs. moral/historical consequence) for Russell's differing evaluations
Distinguishes Russell's own Layer 1 evaluative commentary from neutral summary of Augustine's views

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Augustine's doctrine of creation ex nihilo with the Platonic-Aristotelian view of God as artificer shaping eternal matter, and explain how this difference generates the problem Augustine's theory of time is designed to solve.
rubric: Correctly states both views of creation
Explains why creation ex nihilo raises the question 'why not sooner?'
Reconstructs Augustine's solution via the timelessness of God and the createdness of time
Notes Russell's own assessment of the theory's originality and limits
